content: Earlier cancer studies may need a second look after researchers found that a drug acts mainly on an unexpected target. An experimental cancer drug already being tested in patients appears to work mainly by blocking a different biological target from the one it was developed to inhibit. The finding emerged from brain cancer research that called into question how the drug, zavondemstat, and a closely related research compound, QC6352, produce their anticancer effects. Both compounds were developed to treat cancers such as colorectal, pancreatic, and prostate cancer by targeting KDM4, a family of proteins that can help cancer cells grow and spread when overactive. The new investigation explored their potential against glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive form of brain cancer. “We tested these compounds to investigate whether they could potentially be repurposed for glioblastoma treatment,” said lead author Professor Lenka Munoz of the University of Sydney School of Medical Sciences and Charles Perkins Centre. “When we tested other KDM4 inhibitors, we found they did not reproduce the anti-cancer effects observed with QC6352. “If blocking KDM4 was driving those effects, we would have expected the other inhibitors to behave similarly. Instead, the results suggested QC6352 was acting through a different mechanism.” To trace that mechanism, the team used patient-derived glioblastoma stem cells, tumor models, and a series of genetic, mechanistic, and molecular experiments. The University of Sydney led the research in collaboration with Goethe University, Oxford University, and the Institute of Cancer Research, London. The results were published in Nature Chemical Biology . “Our study found much of the anti-cancer activity of these compounds is driven by blocking DHODH rather than KDM4,” Munoz said. DHODH is an enzyme that cancer cells rely on to produce molecules needed for rapid growth. Blocking it interferes with the supply of materials needed for DNA production. “We can think of DHODH as a machine producing bricks needed to build new DNA. If you switch off the machine, the cell starts running out of bricks and can no longer efficiently copy its DNA and keep dividing,” Munoz said. The findings point to DHODH inhibition as a possible approach to treating glioblastoma. Several drugs that target the enzyme are already being investigated for other cancers, raising the possibility that they could eventually be tested in patients with brain cancer. The current findings come from cells and tumor models, however, and do not establish that these drugs would benefit patients with glioblastoma. The implications also extend to experiments that have used QC6352 to investigate what KDM4 does in cancer. “Researchers around the world have used QC6352 as a leading tool to study KDM4 biology, while the related drug zavondemstat progressed into clinical trials based on the same understanding,” Munoz said. If effects attributed to KDM4 inhibition were largely caused by blocking DHODH, earlier studies using QC6352 may need to be reinterpreted. To help researchers distinguish the two, the team developed new compounds that inhibit KDM4 without affecting DHODH. Those compounds could allow scientists to investigate KDM4’s role more accurately. For zavondemstat’s ongoing clinical development, the findings raise questions about whether trials are being designed around the biological process responsible for much of the drug’s activity. “Getting a drug’s mechanism wrong can lead to poorly designed clinical trials, inappropriate patient selection and years of research focused on the wrong biological target,” Munoz said. “There are well-known examples of cancer drugs advancing through large clinical trials before researchers realized they were not working through the mechanism originally proposed. “Our study shows this is not just a historical problem but one still happening today. Greater rigor is needed to ensure we understand exactly how potential treatments work before they move into clinical testing. “Establishing a drug’s true mechanism early can protect patients, prevent wasted research effort, and help ensure what limited funding we have is directed towards genuinely promising treatments.” Reference: “DHODH is the key target of the KDM4 inhibitor QC6352 in glioblastoma stem cells” by Jayden R. Gomez, Ashwini Patil, Diana D. Shi, Julie-Aurore Losman, Angus J. Saxton, Jennifer R. Baker, Zhihe Lei, Matthew T. O. Holland, Paul E. content: For people with blood cancers called myelodysplastic syndromes, osteoporosis may hold an overlooked clue to survival, a three-year observational study suggests. In blood cancers that develop in the bone marrow, an important clue to a patient’s survival may lie in the bones themselves. Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), a group of cancers that primarily affect older adults, interfere with the body’s ability to produce healthy blood cells. Treatment typically focuses on managing anemia, monitoring blood counts, and providing transfusions when necessary. However, new research suggests that bone health, an often-overlooked aspect of MDS care, may reveal important information about patients’ overall health and prognosis. In a three-year study involving 111 patients with MDS and 84 age-matched control participants, researchers found that people with MDS had significantly lower bone density at the outset and continued to lose bone mass over time. More notably, patients who already had osteoporosis at the beginning of the study also had poorer overall survival. Although the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, they point to a potentially important connection between bone deterioration and blood cancer outcomes. “In patients with MDS, the bone-aging process seems to be sped up,” says Prof. Lorenz Hofbauer, director of the University Center for Healthy Aging at Dresden University Hospital. MDS is among the most common cancers of the blood-forming system. Several thousand people receive an MDS diagnosis in Germany each year. Its incidence rises from approximately 4 to 5 cases per 100,000 people in the general population to more than 30 per 100,000 among people older than 70. “The results are crucial to our understanding of aging processes,” says Hofbauer. “MDS occurs primarily in elderly individuals, precisely during a phase of life in which bone mass, muscle strength, and physical reserves also decline. Often, there is a chronic, subtle inflammatory process present without there being any apparent cause or infection. In addition, MDS is frequently associated with heart attacks and Alzheimer’s disease.” Within blood-forming cells, a specific mutation in the DNMT3A gene was associated with lower bone density, providing another connection for researchers to investigate between blood formation and bone health. Participants with low bone density or osteoporosis were also more likely to have low calcium levels. Hofbauer initiated BoHemE in 2016 with Prof. Uwe Platzbecker, Chief Medical Officer of Dresden University Hospital and a specialist in hematology and oncology. The study involved Dresden and Leipzig University Hospitals, along with other partners in Germany. The findings open opportunities to investigate how blood formation, aging, and bone metabolism influence one another. This is a systems medicine approach, which examines relationships among biological systems and clinical diseases. Collaboration among specialists in blood disorders, bone health, orthopedics, trauma surgery, computer science, and evidence-based medicine could help uncover further connections and support both research and patient care, particularly for older adults with complex conditions. “The message of the BoHemE study is clear: If you want to treat MDS comprehensively, you should also keep an eye on bone health,” says Hofbauer. “Strong bones, a high degree of mobility, and a maintained quality of life are part of a healthy aging process and should be systematically taken into account during the diagnosis and ongoing management of MDS. The Osteoporosis Center at Dresden University Hospital provides suitable treatment options for the individualized management of bone diseases in MDS patients.” Reference: “Bone health in myelodysplastic neoplasms: results from the prospective longitudinal BoHemE study” by Heike Weidner, Elena Tsourdi, Anne Sophie Platzbecker, Martina Rauner, Ulrike Baschant, Maria G. Ledesma-Colunga, Karolina Basiak, Katja Sockel, Ekaterina Balaian, Susann Winter, Anna Harig, Klaus H. Metzeler, Katharina S.
